hub.description: Decks and fences for La Vergne, TN homes, from starter house backyards and rental properties to sloped lots near Percy Priest Lake.
hub.intro: La Vergne sits on I 24 between Nashville and Murfreesboro, with Percy Priest Lake along its northern edge. The houses here are a mix of first homes on modest lots, rentals, and newer builds whose backyards are still bare grass, so most projects come with a firm budget. A landlord needs something tenants will not wear out quickly, while a first time buyer wants solid posts and footings without spending the savings. If your lot runs toward the lake, the first question is where it actually ends. This page covers the basics for La Vergne and links to the deck and fence pages for the details.

sections.heading: The houses behind most La Vergne projects
paragraphs: Many La Vergne projects begin at a first home with a modest yard and a real budget. Often the back door opens onto a small concrete stoop or a couple of wood steps, with bare grass beyond. That is a fine starting point for a simple ground level deck or a straight run of privacy fence. The smart move is to spend on the parts that are hard to redo, like footings and posts, and hold off on extras you can add later.

Rental houses are the other big group, and La Vergne has plenty of them. Landlords tend to ask how a fence or deck will hold up with tenants and whether it can be fixed a board at a time. Newer builds raise different questions. The builder graded the lot and put down sod, then left the rest to you, often with nothing between your patio and the house behind. Whether you live in Stones River Estates or rent out a house near Waldron Road, a La Vergne project starts with what is already in the yard.

sections.heading: Decks for La Vergne homes
paragraphs: On many La Vergne starter homes and newer builds, the back door sits a few steps above the grass. That means even a small deck usually needs stairs, and depending on its height, a railing too. A simple rectangle in pressure treated pine is usually the most budget friendly shape. Composite decking costs more up front but skips the regular staining, a trade some landlords and busy commuters are glad to make.

Some lots closer to Percy Priest Lake slope away from the house, which can turn a modest deck into a tall one. That means longer posts and more bracing, and a taller deck can get a closer look at permit review. Our page for a [deck builder in La Vergne](/deck-builder-la-vergne-tn/) goes deeper into footings in local rock and decks built for rental use. It also covers what to ask a La Vergne builder before you sign.

sections.heading: Fences for La Vergne yards
paragraphs: For many La Vergne homeowners, privacy is the main reason to fence. Newer subdivisions put houses fairly close together, and an open backyard can feel like a shared lawn until a fence goes up. A wood privacy fence in board on board or shadowbox style blocks the view well. Dog owners want pickets close to the ground and a gate that latches on its own. Landlords with pet friendly leases want the same, plus parts that are easy to replace between tenants.

Owners near I 24 in La Vergne sometimes hope a fence will cut road noise. A solid fence hides the traffic, but a wood fence will not quiet an interstate much, so plan it as a screen rather than a sound wall. Our page on [fence installation in La Vergne](/fence-company-la-vergne-tn/) covers property lines and post holes in rocky ground. It also covers lots near the lake.

sections.heading: Ground and water around La Vergne
paragraphs: La Vergne is in a part of Middle Tennessee where limestone is often not far below the surface. Across much of Rutherford County, a post hole or footing can hit rock before it reaches the depth the plan calls for. Where the soil runs deeper, it is usually clay that stays soggy after heavy rain and shrinks as it dries in late summer. Neither one stops a project, but both affect the digging and the estimate, so ask any contractor how they handle rock.

Percy Priest Lake, along the north side of La Vergne, is managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Much of the land around its shore is public, so a yard that seems to run down to the water may end well before it. Check where your line stops before you plan a fence along the back or a deck out toward the view. Past that line, the Corps decides what is allowed.

sections.heading: Rules to check before you build in La Vergne
paragraphs: Permits depend on where your property actually sits. A La Vergne mailing address does not always mean you are inside city limits, and the city and Rutherford County each have their own codes office. Call the one that covers your lot and ask whether your deck or fence needs a permit. Rules vary and change over time, so get the answer from the office itself, not from a neighbor who built in La Vergne a few years ago.

Many newer subdivisions have an HOA with its own review, and that approval is a separate step from any permit. Older La Vergne streets are less likely to have one, but your closing papers will say for sure. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) walks through a clean submission. Before anyone digs, call Tennessee 811 to have buried utility lines marked.

faqs.q: Should I build the deck or the fence first?
faqs.a: It depends on what bothers you most. If you have a dog or a clear view into a neighbor's yard, the fence usually comes first. When the back door drops onto bare dirt, the deck may matter more. Planning both? Lay them out together so the fence leaves room for the deck stairs and the gate lines up with the path you actually walk. That saves tearing out a section of fence later.

faqs.q: Is a deck or fence worth adding to a La Vergne rental?
faqs.a: Many landlords think so. A fenced yard opens the house to tenants with dogs, and a deck makes a small house feel larger. The key is building for wear. Choose materials that can be repaired a piece at a time and hardware rated for treated lumber. On gates, self closing hinges save a lot of trouble. A well built fence or deck should not turn into a constant repair call.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before asking for an estimate in La Vergne?
faqs.a: A rough idea of where the deck or fence should go is enough to start. If your closing papers include a plat or survey, keep it handy, since it shows your lot lines. Note any HOA rules you already know about. Photos of the back of the house and the yard help too, especially on a slope or a lot near the lake. Then send it through the [estimate form](#estimate).

deck.description: Deck builder in La Vergne, TN for starter homes, rentals, and newer builds, with footings planned around local rock and sloped lake lots.
deck.intro: Most La Vergne deck projects start with a practical goal and a set budget. A first time buyer may simply want a place to sit out back. On a rental, the deck has to survive a few rounds of tenants who will not baby it. In a newer build, the family usually wants off the builder's small landing and onto something big enough for a table. The sections below take those jobs one at a time, then cover the permit questions to settle before you hire a deck builder in La Vergne.

sections.heading: Getting the most deck for a La Vergne starter home
paragraphs: On a modest budget, the shape and height of a deck matter more than almost anything else. A low rectangle close to the ground uses less framing and fewer steps, and depending on its height and your codes office, it may not need a railing. Each extra corner or change in level adds labor. Pressure treated pine is usually the least expensive board and holds up well when kept clean and sealed. If you may want composite someday, the frame can be built with that in mind.

Size is where many La Vergne budgets get stretched. For a lot of households, a deck that fits a grill and a table for four is plenty. It is fine to build a solid first stage now and add on later, as long as the footings and the house connection are planned for it. Our guide on [what drives the cost of a deck](/guides/deck-cost-middle-tennessee/) shows how to compare bids line by line, so a low number does not hide a missing stair or railing.

sections.heading: Decks on La Vergne rental houses
paragraphs: La Vergne has a good share of rental houses, and a deck on a rental needs to forgive some neglect. Tenants may not sweep off wet leaves or mention it when a board starts to feel soft. That makes what is under the surface matter most: framing rated for ground contact where it sits low, and fasteners made for treated lumber so they do not rust through. Railings and stair treads take the hardest use, so they are worth checking first.

With an older deck on a rental, the question is usually repair or replace. Gray boards and a few loose screws are a small fix. Rot at the ledger, where the deck meets the house, is not, and neither are posts standing in soil that stays wet. Our guide on [signs your deck is done](/guides/signs-you-need-a-new-deck/) covers what to look for. For La Vergne landlords, the gap between tenants is the easiest time to check.

sections.heading: Footings in La Vergne clay and limestone
paragraphs: Many La Vergne yards have clay on top and limestone below it. How far down the rock sits changes from one yard to the next, and sometimes from one corner of a deck to the other. A footing hole that hits rock early has to be handled on purpose, not filled in and forgotten. Depending on what the codes office accepts, that may mean bearing on the rock or shifting the footing a little. Any deck builder should explain how they handle it and how it shows up in the price.

The clay holds water after a heavy spring rain and shrinks back as it dries in late summer. A footing set too shallow in that soil can move over a few seasons, which shows up as stairs pulling away or a deck that no longer sits level. Footing depth is set by code, and the right depth is the one your codes office signs off on. Keeping water moving away from the posts helps the whole frame last.

sections.heading: Decks on sloped lots near the lake in La Vergne
paragraphs: Lots that fall toward Percy Priest Lake can be steep. A house that sits close to the ground out front can have its back door a full story above the yard once the ground drops toward the water. The view from up there can be worth it, but a taller deck is a bigger job. Posts run longer and need bracing, and a stair down to the yard takes real space. Expect the permit review to look more closely at a deck that high.

Before you plan a deck reaching toward the water, find out where your lot ends. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers manages Percy Priest, and much of the land along the shore is public even where it looks like part of your yard. Building on that land is generally not allowed. A deck kept inside your line goes through the same La Vergne permit process as any other.

sections.heading: Replacing the builder's landing on a newer home
paragraphs: In a newer La Vergne subdivision, the back door often opens onto a small landing and a short set of stairs, enough to get out of the house and not much more. A real deck starts with a ledger fastened to the house framing correctly and flashed so water cannot get behind it. Footings near the house should reach past the loose fill pushed against the foundation, since that fill can keep settling for a while. Also look at how rain leaves the yard. Many newer lots carry water around the house in a shallow channel in the grass, and skirting that runs to the ground can dam it. If you have an HOA, get its rules on placement and color before the design is final.

sections.heading: Permits and questions to ask a La Vergne deck builder
paragraphs: Attached and raised decks usually need a permit, and the review tends to look hard at the footings and at how the deck connects to the house. When you sell, a buyer's inspector may ask whether the deck was permitted. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains how inspections usually work. An HOA review, if you have one, is a separate approval.

When you talk to a deck builder, start with who pulls the permit and who meets the inspector. Then find out what happens if a footing hole hits rock. Tearing out an old deck is easy to leave off a bid, so check whether it is included. Board and fastener choices should come with a reason. For owners in Lake Forest, Stones River Estates, or anywhere else in La Vergne, a bid that skips those points can grow once work starts.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a deck in La Vergne?
faqs.a: In most cases an attached or raised deck needs one, but the details depend on where your property sits and what you are building. Inside city limits, check with the city of La Vergne. Outside them, Rutherford County is usually the office to call, and a mailing address alone will not tell you which applies. Ask before any work starts.

faqs.q: What deck material makes sense for a La Vergne rental house?
faqs.a: Pressure treated pine is the usual choice for rentals because it costs less and a damaged board is easy to swap. It does need cleaning and sealing on a schedule, and tenants rarely do that, so plan it into your own upkeep. Composite costs more up front and skips the staining, which some landlords prefer. Either way the framing underneath is treated lumber, so the fasteners and footings matter as much as the boards.

faqs.q: My back door is several steps above the yard. Does that mean a big deck?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A deck at that height usually needs stairs and a railing, but it does not have to be large. Often the most budget friendly fix for a tall back door is a modest deck at door level with a straight run of stairs. On lots that fall toward the lake, the height grows quickly, so measure before settling on a design.

faqs.q: My La Vergne lot backs toward Percy Priest Lake. How far can the deck go?
faqs.a: Only as far as your property line, and near the lake that line can stop well short of the shore. Much of the shoreline is public land managed by the Corps of Engineers. Check your survey or plat, and contact the Corps before planning anything that reaches toward the water. A deck on your side of the line can still be laid out to face the view.

faqs.q: Is composite decking worth it for a La Vergne deck in full sun?
faqs.a: It can be. Composite does not need staining and will not splinter, which suits busy owners and some landlords. The tradeoff is cost and heat. In full afternoon sun, composite gets hotter underfoot than wood, and darker colors get hotter still. For a west facing deck with no shade, a lighter color or pressure treated pine may be more comfortable. Our comparison of [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) covers how each one ages in Tennessee weather.

fence.description: Privacy fence and rental yard fencing in La Vergne, TN, with post holes planned for local rock and lot lines checked near Percy Priest Lake.
fence.intro: A fence in La Vergne usually has one clear job. In a newer subdivision, it is privacy from the houses behind and beside you. On a rental, it is keeping a tenant's dog in the yard through a few leases. A first time buyer often wants the most fence the budget allows without cutting corners on posts. Near Percy Priest Lake, nothing should go in until you know where your land stops. This page walks through each case, then covers the rock, property line and permit questions that come up during fence installation in La Vergne.

sections.heading: Privacy fences in La Vergne subdivisions
paragraphs: In many La Vergne subdivisions, backyards run open from one lot to the next, and the house behind you may look straight into your kitchen. A full height wood privacy fence is the usual answer. Board on board gives the most complete screen, because the boards overlap and no gaps open as the wood shrinks. Shadowbox alternates boards on either side of the rails, so it looks finished from both yards and lets some breeze through.

With houses this close, your fence is in plain view of several neighbors. Talk with them before work starts. It heads off surprises, and a shared line sometimes turns into a shared cost. Many HOAs expect the finished side to face out, so check before the layout is set. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares the common styles for how much they hide and how they stand up to wind.

sections.heading: Fencing a La Vergne rental
paragraphs: Rentals are common in La Vergne, and for a landlord a fence is mostly about pets. A fenced yard makes a house easier to rent to people with dogs, but only if the fence really holds them. Gaps along the bottom are the usual escape route, so keep the pickets close to the ground. The gate usually wears first. Self closing hinges and a latch that catches on its own keep it shut when a tenant forgets. Our guide to [the best fence for dogs](/guides/best-fence-for-dogs/) covers diggers and jumpers.

Whether the La Vergne rental is in Lake Forest or off Waldron Road, being easy to repair matters more than looks. Pickets that can be swapped one at a time are simple to keep up between tenants. Posts decide how long the whole fence lasts, so they deserve the best lumber in the job. Stain helps wood last, but on a rental it often gets skipped, so pick a fence that still looks fine once it weathers to gray.

sections.heading: Property lines come before fence installation
paragraphs: Every fence installation should start with knowing where the line is. In newer La Vergne subdivisions the corner pins may still be in the ground, though landscaping can hide them. On older lots, a fence or hedge may have stood a little off the line for years. A plat from your closing papers is a start, and a survey settles it. Moving a fence after a neighbor objects costs far more than measuring first.

Call Tennessee 811 before any post hole is dug. The marks show where buried utility lines run, and in many subdivisions those lines follow the back or side of the lot, right where a fence goes. A fence built in a utility easement may have to come down if the utility needs access. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) covers what to do before the first hole.

sections.heading: Post holes in La Vergne rock and clay
paragraphs: Rock is often what slows fence work around La Vergne. Limestone can sit a short way under the clay here, and a line of post holes may go smoothly for a stretch and then hit a ledge. A hole that stops short has to be dealt with, usually by drilling into the rock or moving the post a little. That takes time and the right equipment, so it is fair for a fence company to price it in.

Clay drains slowly, so after a storm a post can sit in a wet pocket well after the lawn looks dry. Over time, that is what rots a wood post at the ground line. Posts treated for ground contact help. So does shaping the top of the concrete so water runs off instead of collecting against the wood. If your yard has a low corner, watch where water sits after a rain before deciding where the posts go.

sections.heading: Lake lots on the north side of La Vergne
paragraphs: If your La Vergne yard backs toward Percy Priest Lake, sort out the back line before anything else. The lake is run by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and much of the ground between private yards and the water is public. A fence that crosses onto it is an encroachment the Corps can make you remove. Find your back corners on a survey and keep the fence inside them. If anything is unclear, ask the Corps staff who manage Percy Priest Lake before you build.

Lots near the lake often slope, and a fence on a hill can be built two ways. Stepped sections stay level and drop down in stairs along the grade, which looks tidy but leaves open triangles at the bottom. Racked sections tilt the rails to follow the ground, which keeps the bottom tight for a dog. Gates on a slope need extra thought so they clear the ground when they swing.

sections.heading: Budget and HOA questions in La Vergne
paragraphs: On a starter home budget, the most cost effective fence is usually a straight run with few corners and one gate. Pressure treated pine is the budget choice, and it does fine here when the posts are set well. You can also fence in stages, closing off the back first for the dog and adding the side sections when the budget allows.

HOA rules deserve their own look. La Vergne subdivisions with an HOA often have covenants on fence style and height, and that review is separate from any city or county permit. Get approval in writing before you schedule anything. Corner lots often have limits near the street so drivers can see, and a fence around a pool comes with its own requirements. Rules vary by address, so confirm yours.

faqs.q: Will a privacy fence block road noise from I 24?
faqs.a: Not by much. A solid privacy fence hides the traffic and headlights, which alone can make a La Vergne yard near the interstate feel calmer. It will not quiet I 24 in any real way, though, since a wood fence is light and has small gaps that let sound through. If noise is the main complaint, treat the fence as a visual screen and plant along the inside to soften things a little more.

faqs.q: Can I fence my yard all the way down to Percy Priest Lake?
faqs.a: Only as far as your own property line, and near the lake that line often stops before the shore. The strip between many private lots and the water is public land managed by the Corps of Engineers. Find the back corners on your survey and keep the fence on your side of them. If the fence would come close to the boundary, check with the Corps first.

faqs.q: Cedar or pressure treated pine for a La Vergne privacy fence?
faqs.a: Both work here. Pressure treated pine costs less and is the common pick on a tight budget, but it tends to shrink and twist a bit as it dries. Cedar is lighter and more stable, and it weathers to a soft gray if left alone. Many fences pair cedar pickets with pressure treated posts, since posts sit in wet ground where treated wood lasts longer. Our guide on [cedar vs pressure treated pine](/guides/cedar-vs-pressure-treated-fence/) goes further.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence in La Vergne?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It depends on where the property is and what kind of fence you are putting up. Inside city limits, the city of La Vergne codes office can tell you. Outside them, check with Rutherford County. A La Vergne mailing address does not always mean the lot is inside the city. If you are in an HOA, its approval is a separate step, and you will want both answers before any posts go in.

faqs.q: Can my new fence connect to my neighbor's fence?
faqs.a: Often it can, but only with your neighbor's agreement and only if their fence is on the line where you think it is. Tying into an old fence also ties your new one to its condition, so if their posts are leaning or rotting, your corner will suffer with them. In La Vergne subdivisions where most yards are fenced, matching heights and styles at the connection makes both look better. Some HOAs have rules on that too.
